transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-03
Time: 09:32 PT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Samira (Redwood SE), Liam (Redwood Product Sec), Aisha (Helios Head Cloud Arch), Marcus (Helios Sec Eng), Priya (Helios Compliance), Diego (Helios Platform)

[00:00] Jordan: Alright hi everyone, thanks for joining. we thought we'd run through Helios' private deployment constraints — network segmentation, egress patterns, firewalling, and then get to KMS/audit logs — make sure we're aligned for the PoC. Samira will drive the technical bits.

[00:17] Aisha: Yep thanks. main ask from our side is: we need to be confident that any outbound internet is strictly controlled. our policy is no direct internet egress from production subnets except through approved proxies and through an outbound egress VPC endpoint. also we need SOC2 coverage and audit trails.

[00:36] Samira: Totally. quick overview: Redwood Private can run in your VPC or on-prem. for VPC deployments we typically use a combination of private subnets for model serving, a dedicated egress layer (we've done both NAT/Gateway+egress proxy and egress-only endpoints), and an optional egress firewall device for allowlisting. our routing can be pinned to specific AZs or across a multi-AZ TGW.

[00:59] Marcus: when you say egress-only endpoints, do you mean AWS PrivateLink-style endpoints? we cannot allow traffic to exit via public IPs except through a monitored appliance.

[01:09] Samira: correct, PrivateLink or interface endpoints for S3, KMS, etc. for outbound model telemetry and optional fallback to hosted models we recommend a managed proxy in a dedicated egress subnet which has strict SGs and NACLs and sits behind an IDS. traffic flows from serving nodes -> egress proxy -> approved external destinations. if you require zero public IPs we can use VPC endpoints to services and an egress appliance that only speaks to curated endpoints.

[01:36] Diego: can you describe how that appliance looks? is it a third-party firewall or something you bring as an AMI?

[01:43] Samira: we've done both. common patterns: 1) customer-managed firewall/NGFW (Palo Alto, Fortinet) in the egress subnet with SNAT to its IPs; 2) an AWS Network Firewall with managed rules; 3) an HA pair of proxy instances (nginx/envoy) with egress ACLs plus an IDS. Redwood's runtime supports routing all outbound through that egress IP range. we also support active health checks and failover.

[02:07] Marcus: ok. logging — we need full connection logs, user identity mapping (which user/API key triggered the request), and immutable audit writes to our SIEM. how does Redwood handle audit logs in Private mode?

[02:20] Liam: answer: audit events are emitted by our control plane agent — they include token id, request route, model version, timestamp, latency, and outcome. in Private mode audit events can be streamed to your S3 (with KMS encryption) or forwarded directly to your Syslog/Graylog/Splunk endpoint over TLS. for high-assurance customers we support signing audit logs and write-once object lifecycle policies.

[02:45] Priya: signing logs sounds good. retention requirements: SOC2 requires 12 months, but we might want 3 years for some PII-related flows. can you support custom retention on those buckets and separation of duties on the KMS keys?

[02:58] Liam: yes — you can supply your own CMKs in KMS or an external HSM. we can ensure logs are encrypted using your key and that Redwood's role has encryption-only and no key deletion privileges. separation of duties is enforced by IAM policies on the bucket and KMS.

[03:14] Aisha: what about RBAC/SSO? we want role mappings that align to our internal AD groups. especially important: who can trigger model rollouts and who can request fallback to hosted models.

[03:25] Jordan: we support SAML/Okta integration for SSO; RBAC is configurable via the console or via an API, and you can map SAML group attributes to roles like admin, engineer, auditor. Samira, any notes on role enforcement at the API layer?

[03:38] Samira: enforcement is at two layers: control plane (deploys, rollouts) uses SAML-backed sessions and role checks; runtime (inference calls) uses API keys or short-lived tokens issued by the control plane with scopes. we also support OIDC token exchange for federated caller identity. tokens include origin info so audit logs tie back to identities.

[03:58] Diego: short-lived tokens — do they have to go through a token broker? we can't have long-lived keys on any compute nodes.

[04:05] Samira: our recommended pattern: run a small token broker service in your control plane; it authenticates service identities (via mTLS or instance profile) and requests scoped short-lived keys from Redwood control plane. those keys expire in minutes. for on-prem we support an agent that rotates ephemeral credentials for the runtime.

[04:25] Marcus: good. a couple of network specifics: we use both Security Groups and NACLs. we want to ensure the KV cache traffic is internal only — not crossing AZ boundaries in a way that requires outbound to the internet. how do you handle KV cache and inter-node replication?

[04:40] Samira: KV/cache traffic is local to the VPC and can be pinned to AZ-local endpoints. we use internal ENIs and private IPs; we don't require public endpoints for replication. for multi-AZ we recommend private peering over TGW and encrypted traffic (TLS). we can also support SR-IOV/ENIs pinned for high-throughput setups.

[05:02] Priya: encryption in transit — is mTLS supported between internal components? and can we inject our own certificates from internal PKI?

[05:11] Samira: yes to both. runtime components support mTLS; you can provide your own cert chain and we can validate against your root CA. that gives you mutual auth across control plane <-> runtime and runtime <-> egress proxies.

[05:25] Aisha: on the firewall rules, we want a deny-by-default posture. the only allowed outbound destinations should be our SIEM, our artifact repo for models, KMS endpoints, and a pinned set of telemetry endpoints. can we get a recommended minimal ACL list?

[05:38] Samira: we'll provide a baseline that includes: allowed TCP/443 to your SIEM IPs (or endpoint), to S3 interface endpoints, to your KMS endpoints, to your internal docker registry/OCI repo, and to the egress proxy's IP. also allow health-checking internal load balancers and control plane API endpoints. everything else denied. we'll include CIDR ranges and FQDNs in the diagram.

[06:01] Marcus: what's the failure mode if the egress proxy is down? we can't accidentally fall back to hosted Redwood API over the public internet.

[06:10] Samira: by default we set the runtime policy to 'hard-fail' — if egress is unavailable, requests fail. we can, however, configure an explicit fallback to a hosted variant but only if you opt in and sign an allowlist. for the PoC we'll keep fallback disabled.

[06:25] Jordan: note for procurement: fallback toggles are in the rollout policy and require admin-level changes; we can tie that to SAML admin groups and require two-person approval to change.

[06:36] Diego: what about DNS leakage? some libraries can do DNS lookups that bypass VPC endpoints.

[06:43] Samira: we recommend DNS controls — use your Route53 Resolver endpoints with outbound rules to only resolve whitelisted domains, and combine with VPC DNS hostnames disabled on host-level for additional safety. we also run a local DNS proxy in the egress subnet to filter requests.

[06:59] Priya: KMS detail: we need HSM-backed keys for encryption at rest for both model artifacts and logs. can Redwood integrate with customer HSM or on-prem Thales?

[07:10] Liam: yes, we have two options: 1) bring-your-own-KMS: Redwood uses your cloud CMK (AWS KMS key) that may be HSM-backed; 2) external HSM via PKCS#11 for on-prem keys — we support a gateway to that HSM for encrypt/decrypt requests. in both cases we can configure key usage policies so Redwood only has Encrypt/Decrypt and not key-manage privileges.

[07:35] Aisha: and secrets handling for model weights or checkpoints — do you store them in our S3 or in local disks? any encryption-at-rest for local caches?

[07:45] Samira: model weights can be stored either: in your S3 bucket (recommended) or on local encrypted volumes. local caches are encrypted with LUKS and keys are wrapped by your CMK. for staging PoC we can use S3 with KMS encryption.

[07:58] Marcus: how about network segmentation for training vs inference? we don't want data exfil from training infra.

[08:06] Samira: Redwood Private is focused on inference, but we can tag nodes and mTLS identities — you can restrict access so training clusters can't reach inference subnets. we'll provide IAM and SG templates for separation.

[08:20] Priya: compliance question — SOC2: will Redwood provide documentation and evidence for the Private deployment, or do we need to collect logs on our side?

[08:30] Jordan: we provide a SOC2 whitepaper and will hand over the control-plane artifacts we own. for customer-managed components you'll need to collect infrastructure logs. typically we export audit logs to your SIEM and give you signed artifacts for audits.

[08:44] Priya: do you do pen tests on the Private agent?

[08:48] Liam: yes we run internal pentests and can share summary reports; for shared infra you may run a limited-scope test with coordination. we also support CVE notifications and a process for patch windows.

[09:00] Aisha: okay let's recap and next steps. we want the following from Redwood: architecture diagram with exact subnets and SG/NACL rules, a minimal ACL whitelist, a lab plan for PoC in our staging VPC, and the SOC2/KMS/HSM documentation. Helios will confirm HSM requirement and grant a test account in staging.

[09:18] Jordan: yes we'll send the diagram and ACLs, samira will coordinate the lab plan, and we'll block the follow-up for 2025-10-21 to review PoC results. any other blockers?

[09:29] Diego: one tiny thing — can you include expected egress bandwidth and token cost estimate for our monthly projected volume? we need to budget.

[09:36] Samira: we'll include a cost snapshot: throughput (tokens/sec), bandwidth, and likely instance sizing for a dedicated pool. Jordan will include that in the follow-up email.

[09:46] Marcus: sounds good. thanks everyone.

[09:50] Jordan: thanks all. we'll follow up with docs and next steps.

[09:55] call ends.
